The Southern African vlei rat, Otomys irroratus, is a medium-sized murid rodent inhabiting moist grasslands and wetlands of the region. Neonates emerge weighing approximately 14.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 14.5 grams], a modest mass typical of altricial mammals that require an extended period of maternal investment. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], the gestation period has been recorded at 40 days [tg = 40 days], a duration consistent with the relatively slow developmental rates observed in several African otomyine rodents when compared to similarly sized murines. This comparatively long gestation is thought to reflect the high degree of neurological and physiological development achieved in utero, which may confer advantages in the predator-rich marsh environments this species occupies. Following parturition, the lactational phase is relatively brief; pups transition to nutritional independence after approximately 13 days since birth [tx = approximately 13 days since birth] at this same body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C]. This rapid weaning timeline suggests that milk composition in this species is exceptionally rich, allowing suckling juveniles to achieve the critical mass required for independent foraging swiftly. The interplay between a short suckling period and a moderate gestation length represents a distinctive life-history strategy within the murid radiation of southern Africa.

Juvenile males and females diverge in their developmental trajectories, with the onset of sexual maturation occurring at different ages. When measured at a core body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], female vlei rats attain puberty at 82 days since birth [tp = 82 days since birth], while male conspecifics reach reproductive maturity somewhat later, at 91 days since birth [tp = 91 days since birth]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is not uncommon among polygynous or promiscuous rodent species, where delayed male maturity may be linked to the energetic demands of establishing a territory or achieving a competitive body size. Sub-adult males undergo a pronounced growth spurt during this period, gradually approaching the ultimate adult body mass. Such a divergence in the pubertal schedule has direct demographic consequences, as it creates a temporal offset between the availability of receptive females and fully fertile males within a population. Field observations confirm that this pattern is robust even under variable environmental conditions, suggesting a genetically canalized developmental program.

The species achieves an ultimate wet weight of 146.8 grams [Wwi = 146.8 grams] in well-nourished adults, a substantial size relative to many other members of the Otomys genus. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually as the growing juvenile transitions from a weaning mass of 30 grams [Wwx = 30 grams] through an extended sub-adult phase. The nearly fivefold increase from birth mass to adult weight reflects sustained, high-quality maternal provisioning coupled with an herbivorous diet of grasses and sedges that provides adequate energetic margins for somatic growth. Large body size in this species is hypothesized to confer advantages in thermoregulation within the cool, high-altitude marshes it frequently colonizes, as well as in intraspecific competition for prime foraging territories. The transition from the weaning stage, when individuals weigh approximately 30 grams [Wwx = approximately 30 grams], to the onset of reproductive activity necessitates a careful balance between continued somatic growth and the initiation of gonadal function. Food availability during this crucial window can significantly influence whether a juvenile successfully reaches the adult mass threshold needed to support breeding.

Reproductive output in Otomys irroratus is best characterized by litter size and breeding frequency rather than a daily rate. Under the stable thermal conditions of a captive colony maintained at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], females typically produce litters containing 1.78 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1.78 pups per litter] and achieve an average of 4.25 litters annually [F_R_i = 4.25 litters annually]. This relatively low reproductive frequency, combined with the modest litter size, suggests a slower-paced life history than many murid rodents, potentially driven by the energetic constraints of producing precocial young that require extensive gestation.

Longevity data for this species remain somewhat uncertain, as recapture rates in mark-recapture studies are often confounded by high juvenile mortality and dispersal. The available evidence, drawn from captive colonies held at a stable temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], suggests that the maximum lifespan is in the vicinity of 3 years [am = 3 years]. However, some isolated field records of marked individuals returning to trapping grids after extended periods hint that under exceptionally favorable conditions, individual vlei rats might survive somewhat longer, perhaps reaching four years of age. This estimated lifespan of 3 years [am = 3 years] is consistent with predictions for a rodent of this body mass and reproductive schedule occupying a relatively stable, albeit seasonally variable, wetland habitat at a temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C]. The species does not exhibit classical signs of reproductive senescence before mortality; instead, geriatric individuals appear to succumb primarily to predation or to the cumulative physiological stress of repeated breeding cycles. The uncertain nature of this lifespan estimate, derived largely from a single captive cohort held at 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], underscores the need for additional longitudinal field studies employing robust telemetry or genetic mark-recapture methods to refine our understanding of natural mortality rates in this ecologically distinctive rodent.
